extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; general literate public (early 18th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: A moral/social periodical essay (Spectator) giving prescriptive judgments about manners, economy, exercise, and rural life aimed at a general literate readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oeconomy vs pretending behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: “Oeconomy in our Affairs has the same Effect upon our Fortunes which Good Breeding has upon our Conversations. There is a pretending Behaviour in both Cases, which, instead of making Men esteemed, renders them both miserable and contemptible.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid affectation of wealth or manners; genuine moderation (economy) earns steadier esteem, whereas pretending produces misery and contempt. The essay contrasts two responses to poverty—shame-driven ostentation and fear-driven frugality—to show both excess and neglect are vices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not maintain an estate beyond your means
rubrics_metrics.description: “To pay for, personate, and keep in a Man's Hands, a greater Estate than he really has, is of all others the most unpardonable Vanity, and must in the End reduce the Man who is guilty of it to Dishonour.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequences listed: sleepless nights, constant inquietudes, danger of affronts, eventual reduction to dishonour. Example figures (Laertes) show how pride in reputation leads to ruin; selling part of an estate to relieve debt is advised over maintaining false appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set a personal spending limit
rubrics_metrics.description: “every Man would point to himself what Sum he would resolve not to exceed.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a conscious limit to personal expenditure to achieve tranquility; surplus above that limit should be converted to nobler uses rather than personal luxury. This is a practical maxim to avoid vain striving and envy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish labour (livelihood) from exercise (pleasure) and value both
rubrics_metrics.description: “Bodily Labour is of two Kinds, either that which a Man submits to for his Livelihood, or that which he undergoes for his Pleasure ... The latter ... differs only from ordinary Labour as it rises from another Motive.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both work for subsistence and voluntary exercise are necessary for health; frequent motions keep bodily systems (metaphorically a 'system of Tubes and Glands') functioning, prevent the spleen and vapours, and support mental faculties. Neglect of physical exercise is implicated in melancholy among sedentary scholars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riding recommended as ideal exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is no kind of Exercise which I would so recommend to my Readers of both Sexes as this of Riding, as there is none which so much conduces to Health...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Endorsed by practical and medical authority (Dr. Sydenham, Medicina Gymnastica). Riding suits the body’s structure and offers mechanical benefits; when in town, alternative exercises (dumb bell routine) are proposed to maintain vigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of moderate sports to preserve health (not to drown thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Citing Pascal: many pursue sports to ‘drown Thought’; proper exercise should serve preservation of health and enable the soul to execute its orders rather than to avoid introspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage in sports as healthful exercise and moderation, not as mere distraction from self-reflection. If sports consume the whole mind, they become blameworthy; if used to keep body and mind fit, they are laudable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humane conduct and discipline in sporting/hunting
rubrics_metrics.description: Account of Sir Roger calling off hounds and sparing a near-caught hare; praise for the discipline of the pack and the Knight’s Good-nature in not murdering an animal that had provided diversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sports should be governed by discipline and benevolence: training of hounds, respect for reputed animals in the pack, and humane treatment of quarry (keeping captured hares alive) are praised as marks of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation of desires / magnanimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise of Mr. Cowley: his magnanimity and moderation of desires render him admirable; moderation is a distinguishing and ennobling temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate moderation in desires to be amiable and content; avoid the pursuit of superfluities once essential needs and reasonable comforts are secured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elite conduct affects public belief (avoid private feuds)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Feuds of this Nature, though too frequent in the Country, are very fatal to the ordinary People; who ... pay as much Deference to the Understanding of a Man of an Estate, as of a Man of Learning ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conflicts between local 'squire' and parson (public quarrels) harm ordinary people by confusing or undermining moral/truthful authority; elites should avoid public contentions that lead tenants to disregard important truths proclaimed by clerics or others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage and encouragement of parish virtue and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of Sir Roger ordering a Bible for a boy who answers well in catechising, giving a flitch of bacon to his mother, adding five pounds a year to the clerk's place, and promising to reward merit on the incumbent's death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Landlords and local leaders should encourage religious and moral education and reward merit (e.g., gifts, increased stipend) to promote good parish conduct; such patronage fosters social harmony and virtue rather than scandal.
